To fix (4)

To fix Power Analysis Check

What we found

We detected 1 potential power analysis.

Show details

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

Some essential information could not be detected: alpha_level, software

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
apriori other 86 NA 0.8 0.43 Cohen’s d NA
text
Following our preregistration, we aimed to recruit 400 participants in total, equally and randomly allocated to 4 versions of an online gamified cognitive task followed by six post-task questionnaires. The sample size was informed by an a priori power calculation based on pilot data, using a t-test comparing learning rates between two second stable blocks from the task (i.e., the stable-to-stable and volatile-to-stable conditions). The observed effect size (d=0.43) indicated that 86 participants per group were required to achieve 80% power. Accordingly, a target of 100 participants for each task condition was set to allow for exclusions while maintaining adequate power. Due to an error during recruitment two versions of the task included 101 participants. Following exclusions, the final sample size for the cognitive task was 330 participants.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 2 imprecise p values out of 8 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p≥0.05 Results indicated that trait anxiety, as well as all other mental health measures, did not significantly predict single or dual learning rate changes after applying FDR correction (p≥0.05).
p>0.05 Regression analyses using these factor scores revealed that none of the four-factor solutions significantly predicted single or dual learning rate change in any of the task versions after applying FDR correction (p>0.05; Tables S9-S10).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To fix Codebook Check

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 5 codebook/README/label sources and 266 data columns across 27 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (33 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents min`, `max, prior_mu_mean`, `prior_mu_sigma, prior_sigma_scale while the data has questionnaire_key, question_id, item_label. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 4 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .055 The interaction between current and previous block volatility was not significant (F(1, 326) = 3.70, p = .055, ηp² = .01), indicating that there was no clear evidence of a difference between stable and volatile current environments in the effect of previous volatility.
p = 1.00 Follow-up t-tests also revealed that this effect was most prominent in the current volatile condition (t(160) = -3.81, corrected p < .001, d = 0.60), while no significant difference was found when comparing conditions where the current block was stable (t(166) = 0.57, corrected p = 1.00, d = 0.09).
p≥0.05 Results indicated that trait anxiety, as well as all other mental health measures, did not significantly predict single or dual learning rate changes after applying FDR correction (p≥0.05).
p>0.05 Regression analyses using these factor scores revealed that none of the four-factor solutions significantly predicted single or dual learning rate change in any of the task versions after applying FDR correction (p>0.05; Tables S9-S10).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Some OSF registrations only describe what was shared, while the actual files live in the project they were registered from — if that project is closed and the registration holds no copy, metacheck cannot list or download its files, and other researchers cannot access them either. Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 24 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 266 columns across 27 data files.

Issues Identified

2 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

File Column Issues
behavioural_data.csv trial_in_block ⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 96882 values are missing
questionnaire_data.csv responseLabel 🔤 Case issues — Categories differing only by case: Not at all/not at all

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 27 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Your code was written for older versions of its packages.

  • make_publication_figures.py: “AttributeError: module ‘matplotlib.style’ has no attribute ‘core’”
  • make_recovery_figures.py: “AttributeError: module ‘matplotlib.style’ has no attribute ‘core’”

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.
  2. State your version of R or Python in the README.
  3. Better still, update the code so it also works with current versions.

A package could not be installed.

  • regression_analysis.py needs stats_utils.

stats_utils could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version.

Other problems in the files

  • test_compile_results.py calls os.chdir(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 2 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: volatility_generalisation/init.py (by make_publication_figures.py, make_recovery_figures.py, regression_analysis.py); volatility_generalisation/figures/init.py (by make_publication_figures.py, make_recovery_figures.py, regression_analysis.py); publication_figures.py (by make_publication_figures.py, make_recovery_figures.py, regression_analysis.py, recovery_figures.py); recovery_figures.py (by make_recovery_figures.py); condition_metadata.py (by make_publication_figures.py, publication_figures.py); data_generation.py (by recovery_figures.py); data_preparation.py (by make_publication_figures.py); integrated_model_recovery.py (by recovery_figures.py); integrated_model_selection.py (by recovery_figures.py); model_simulation.py (by publication_figures.py); plotting.py (by regression_analysis.py); posterior_utils.py (by publication_figures.py). os.chdir() in the code

6 scripts call os.chdir(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with pass. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring an os.chdir() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

We use a gamified decisionmaking task (Sookud et al., 2026) in which participants are presented with two temporally and perceptually distinct environments, enabling current and prior environmental volatility to be manipulated factorially, to establish how exposure to a prior environment affects learning in the current setting.

All participants were recruited via the online platform Prolific.

Eligible participants were those who were based in the UK, aged 18 or older to ensure informed consent could be provided, and had an acceptance rate of >=98% on Prolific.

All participants were compensated for their time at a rate of £9 per hour for completion of the study.

Participants were instructed to choose between two cannon-ball containers, each associated with a reward probability that varied across the task.

Participants were also required to aim at the alien, although this behaviour was only included as part of the cover story.

Participants completed only one task version to avoid carry-over effects between conditions.

Since we were interested in how learning rates generalise across distinct contexts, participants were presented with the message “You have now entered a new environment” before entering the second block, which had a visually distinct layout from the first block (see Figure 1), ensuring that participants perceived a significant change in the environmental context.

Once participants completed the task, they were asked to provide basic demographic information (age and sex), followed by a series of six questionnaires assessing common mental health problems, related symptoms, and personality traits: State-Trait Inventory of Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA) (Boyer & Rodieck, 2017; Grös et al., 2007), Intolerance to Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12) (Carleton et al., 2007), Patient Health Questionnaire 8 item (PHQ-8) (Spitzer et al., 1999), Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7 item scale (GAD-7) (Spitzer et al., 2006), Revised Life Oriented Test (LOT-R) (Scheier et al., 1994), and Transdiagnostic symptoms inventory (Hopkins et al., 2022).

Participants were excluded for inattentive task behaviour if they 1) selected one cannon on >=75% of trials, given that both options are equally rewarding across the task, or 2) exhibited a standard deviation of a 10-trial choice moving average of <0.2 (low-variance responding).

We recruited a sample of 402 participants.

As expected, an ANOVA revealed that current block volatility (F(1, 326) = 10.04, p = .002, ηp² = .03) had a significant positive effect on learning rate derived from the Rescorla-Wagner learning model, such that learning rates were higher when participants were currently in a volatile environment.

However, and in line with our hypothesis, we also observed a significant effect of previous block volatility (F(1, 326) = 7.72, p = .006, ηp² = .02, Figure 3), indicating that learning rates were higher when participants had previously experienced a volatile environment.

Each participant completed one of four versions, each providing a unique combination of stable and volatile conditions across the two blocks.

Ethics approval statement:

This study was ethically approved by the King’s College London Research Ethics Committee (LRU/RGO-25/26-52823).

research_questions Our primary research questions and corresponding hypotheses are as follows:

Q1) How do learning styles generalise across different environments with varying uncertainty?

Hypothesis (H1): Prior block effects and computational learning parameters
Learning rate, estimated using a Rescorla-Wagner model fitted to participants’ choice behaviour and associated reward outcomes, will differ between blocks in each task version. Specifically, learning rates in the second block will reflect carryover effects from the first block, indicating generalisation of learning styles across environmental contexts. Based on pilot experiments, we expect this effect to be specific to stable environments (i.e., stable environments will be affected by prior experience), although we will also test for effects in volatile blocks as additional exploratory analyses.

Q2) Does trait anxiety influence the extent to which learning styles generalise across different environments?

Hypothesis 2 (H2): Exploratory analyses of trait anxiety
Trait anxiety (STICSA scores) will be examined as a continuous predictor of computational indices of generalisation (i.e., difference in learning rates) across blocks for each task version. Although these analyses are exploratory, based on prior literature we expect trait anxiety level to be a significant predictor of learning rate changes across task blocks.
foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
study_type Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
intention_for_causal_interpretation Direct inference on causal relationship(s): This study is intended to infer or estimate a causal relationship between two or more variables. It is designed specifically for the purposes of causal inference or identification.
blinding No blinding is involved.
study_design_overview Each participant is randomly assigned to complete 1 out of 4 versions of a online gamified cognitive task (the cannonball task), which is in essence a 2-armed bandit. In this task, participants are asked to choose between two stimuli (a left or right cannon), each of which are predictive of reward (a cannonball that makes it to its target without exploding) to some extent, to earn as many points as possible. This is repeated for multiple different combinations of pairs of stimuli, and therefore involves trial-and-error learning.

Version 1 of the task begins with a volatile block of 120 trials, in which the reward probability associated with one of two cannons switches every 20 trials. This is followed by a stable block of 120 trials, where the reward probability switches every 60 trials. To ensure participants perceive a significant change in environmental context, they are shown the message “You have now entered a new environment” before entering the second block, which has a visually distinct layout from the first block.

Version 2 of the task uses the same statistical structure but reverses the order, starting with the stable block followed by the volatile block. Counterbalancing the order of these blocks/environmental contexts allows us to manipulate participants’ initial prior beliefs and examine how these priors generalise when environmental statistics change. However, despite such counterbalancing, participants will only complete one version of the task, as completing both would introduce substantial carry over effects (i.e., learning from the first task version would bias performance in the second).

As control conditions, version 3 of the task begins with a volatile block of 120 trials followed by another volatile block of 120 trials, while version 4 begins with a stable block of 120 trials followed by another stable block of 120 trials. This ensures that the effects observed in versions 1 and 2 of the task can be attributed to changes in environmental volatility and block order.

Once participants complete the task they are instructed to complete a series of six questionnaires online, assessing relevant psychological traits of interest, including:

- Sate-Trait Inventory of Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA): This will be used to measure trait anxiety.
- Intolerance to Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12): This will be used to assess sensitivity to uncertainty (and compared to individuals’ task performance).
- Patient Health Questionnaire 8 item (PHQ-8): This will be used to control for high depressive symptoms.
- Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7 item scale (GAD-7): This will be used to control for high depressive symptoms.
- Revised Life Oriented Test (LOT-R): This will be used to measure general expectations about positive and negative outcomes.
- Transdiagnostic symptoms inventory (Hopkins et al., 2022): This will be used as a brief measure of additional transdiagnostic mental health symptoms.

Scores obtained from these questionnaires will allow us to identify the extent to which anxiety scores (individuals with lower- vs higher-trait anxiety) influence task performance (generalisation effects), while accounting for other mental health characteristics.

Consequently, this study uses a mixed factorial design. Task version is manipulated between subjects, such that each participant completes only one version of the cannonball task (versions 1-4), while environmental context (volatile vs. stable blocks) is manipulated within subjects, allowing behaviour to be compared across contexts within each task version. Additionally, trait anxiety is not treated as a categorical grouping variable but instead measured continuously and incorporated into regression analyses. Specifically, individual anxiety scores (from the STICSA questionnaire) are used to predict learning-related parameters (i.e., Learning Rate) estimated from task performance, to examine if and how anxiety modulates behavioural adaptation and generalisation across environmental contexts. Together, the combination of these between- and within-subject components constitute a mixed factorial design.

Following the behavioural analysis of participants’ learning patterns across environmental contexts, a computational model based on the Rescorla-Wagner framework and Hierarchical Bayesian modelling will be applied to the task data. This model will be used to estimate key learning parameters, including learning rate, with the aim of reproducing the belief updating patterns observed from participants’ behaviour/performance in the task. Since both the task and computational model rely on model-free learning (i.e., learning through trial and error), this allows us to effectively observe how prior belief updating evolves over time and across environmental contexts (aligning with our aims and hypotheses).
data_collection_procedures Participants will be recruited through the online platform Prolific, which allows access to a large and diverse participant pool. Broad inclusion criteria will be applied in the aim of obtaining a representative sample. Specifically, eligible participants must be based in the UK, aged 18 or older to ensure informed consent can be provided, and must have an acceptance rate of >=98% on Prolific, indicating a history of reliable, high-quality responses and ensuring data integrity. No additional exclusion criteria will be applied.
sample_size Based on pilot data and power analyses, we aim to recruit up to 100 participants per task version. However, because participants who fail to complete all trials or show evidence of inattentive responding (i.e., random responding on >=75% of trials) will be excluded from statistical analyses, the final sample sizes across task versions/conditions are not expected to be equal, but anticipated to fall within the range of approximately 90-100 participants for each task version.
sample_size_rationale The sample size is based on a power calculation using effect sizes from a pilot study based on a t-test on learning rates between the two second stable blocks (i.e., from the stable > stable and volatile > stable conditions), where an effect size of d=0.43 indicates that 86 participants in each group are required for 80% power. Our target of 100 per group allows for exclusions, and we also include 100 participants for all conditions to allow testing of effects on volatile blocks (although strong effects were not observed here in piloting).
stopping_rule Data collected during pilot testing will not be included in the analyses reported in this study. Formal data collection for the study will begin once the finalised task is deployed and participant recruitment begins via Prolific.

Data collection will terminate once 100 participants per task version have been obtained.
manipulated_variables The independent variables in the current study include trait anxiety score, task version, and environmental context. Specifically, trait anxiety is measured using each participants’ STICSA post-task questionnaire scores and is treated as a continuous individual-difference variable. These scores are incorporated into between-subject regression analyses to examine how variation in trait anxiety relates to task performance.

Task version is a between-subjects factor, with participants completing either Version 1 (volatile-to-stable), Version 2 (stable-to-volatile), Version 3 (volatile-to-volatile), or Version 4 (stable-to-stable) of the adapted cannonball task. In contrast, environmental context is a within-subjects factor, as all participants experience both volatile and stable blocks within their assigned task version, allowing us to examine the effects of each block on participants’ performance.

With regards to the computational model, the independent variables include task version and environmental context, as these define the statical structure of the learning environment and drive belief updating. Trait anxiety, however, is not modelled as an independent variable within the model itself; instead, it is treated as a continuous individual-difference measure and used in regression analyses of the model’s estimated parameters (learning rate) to assess whether variation in anxiety modulates learning dynamics.

These independent variables allow us to investigate how individual differences in anxiety and the type of environmental statistics influence learning, belief updating, and generalisation (the primary dependent variables).

However, although the primary focus is on comparing low- to high-trait anxious individuals and their distinct belief updating patterns, participants with elevated depression scores (from post-task questionnaires) will not be excluded from the study. Including these participants allows us to account for variance associated with depressive symptoms while isolating trait anxiety-specific effects on belief updating. Incorporating depression as a covariate therefore controls for potential confounding effects, ensuring that observed differences can be confidently attributed to trait anxiety.
measured_variables The primary dependent variables in this study are derived from participants’ performance in the adapted cannonball task, specifically choice behaviour as well as the trial outcome (i.e., if the cannonball exploded or not for a given choice) for training the computational model. Our primary measure is the degree of generalisation between environmental contexts (e.g., volatile-to-stable vs. stable-to-volatile blocks) as estimated based on the learning rate parameter from a Rescorla-Wagner model, including learning rate.

We will also run exploratory analyses using other computational models (e.g., dual learning rate models or Pearce-Hall models), and may also look at metrics derived from choice behaviour directly (e.g., choice variability).
indices Computational indices are derived by fitting a Rescorla–Wagner model (using hierarchical Bayesian modelling) to participants’ trial-by-trial choice behaviour and outcome data (i.e., whether the cannonball exploded or not on a given trial). The primary model-derived parameter of interest is the learning rate (α), which is estimated separately for each environmental context within each task version.
statistical_tests For computational modelling analyses, learning rates (α) are estimated independently for each block within each task version using the Rescorla-Wagner model. To address our primary research questions, participants’ behavioural data including choice (trial-by-trial switching) will be statistically analysed ANOVAs and t-tests. Between-subject ANOVAs will be conducted to compare choice behaviour across each task version. Therefore, Hypothesis 1 (H1) will be tested by assessing whether first-block performance predicts second-block performance, and therefore whether learning in the initial environment generalises to the subsequent environment. To achieve this, an ANOVA will be specified that uses data from only the 2nd blocks, with prior and current block type (as well as their interaction) as independent variables. H1 will be tested by 1) examining the main effect of prior block on learning rates, and 2) via a t-test comparing learning rates in the two 2nd stable blocks, given that we expect the effect to be specific to stable environments.

These analyses directly address H1 and H2 by testing whether learning rates generalise across environmental contexts (e.g., from the first to the second block) and whether this generalisation differs as a function of block order and environmental structure.

Finally, to examine the relationship between learning dynamics and trait anxiety (H3), Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression analyses will be conducted with difference in learning rates between 1st and 2nd blocks as the dependent variable and STICSA scores as a continuous predictor variable. These regression analyses will be performed separately for each task version to assess whether individual differences in anxiety predict variation in learning rates across environmental contexts. Together, these analyses allow us to assess both the generalisation of learning across environments (H1) and the extent to which trait anxiety modulates learning dynamics (H2).
transformations Learning rates will be subject to a logit transform for analyses using this variable as the dependent variable.
inference_criteria Statistical significance for all ANOVAs, t-tests, and regression analyses will be evaluated using a two-tailed criteria of <0.05. Effect sizes will be reported using partial η² for ANOVAs, Cohen’s d for t-tests, and standardised regression coefficients for OLS analyses.
data_exclusion_criteria Participants who fail to complete all trials of the task or questions from post-task questionnaires we be excluded from analyses. Additionally, participants who show evidence of inattentive responding in the task or failing more than 1 infrequency item in the questionnaires (where the 1st and 2nd most “correct” answers are treated as correct) will be excluded.

Inattentive task behaviour will be determined as 1) selecting one option on >= 75% of trials, given that across the task both options are equally as rewarding, and 2) exhibiting low-variance responding (assessed by having a standard deviation of a 10-trial choice moving average of < 0.2, reflective of little learning).
missing_data_handling Any missing data from participants will result in the given participant being removed from the data when carrying out analyses.
